blocks.title: The machine teaches too
blocks.html: Try running wok(7 / 2). A calculator says 3.5 — JRG answers 3, because dividing two whole numbers gives a whole number. Differences like that are shown, not hidden.

lines.html: 1. Read the error message to the end — it names the line and often gives a suggestion
2. Try it in the editor: change one thing, run, see the difference
3. Delete half the code until the error disappears — what you removed last is the cause

blocks.html: The third step sounds trivial and is actually the most powerful. Chapter JRG 12 goes deeper into it.

blocks.title: Ready?
blocks.html: If you are completely new, open JRG Basics — Chapter 1 in the menu on the left. If you want to go straight to math, open Basic Arithmetic. There is no wrong order — the only wrong move is stopping before you have run a single piece of code.

content.title: First Program
content.subtitle: Writing, running, and reading the result. No math in this chapter — just making sure you can get the computer to follow one sentence.

blocks.html: A program is a list of commands carried out in order, from top to bottom. The most basic command in JRG is wok — it means “write this to the screen”.
Three things there, and only one of them really does the work:

rows: The way in. JRG starts reading here.
Curly braces fence in the body of the function. Everything inside belongs to main.
Write to the screen, then move to a new line.

blocks.title: Why is it called wok?
blocks.html: A short word that is easy to say, and deliberately short because it is the command you will write most while learning. Its counterparts are print in Python, console.log in JavaScript, and println! in Rust.
wok accepts more than one value. The values are separated by spaces automatically.

blocks.title: wok_ without a new line
blocks.html: To continue on the same line, use wok_ (with the underscore). Handy for printing numbers side by side.
A line starting with // is not run by the computer. Use it to explain why, not to repeat what.

JRG does not stay quiet when your program is wrong. It names the line, points at the column, and gives a suggestion. Try a deliberate mistake (error messages are in Indonesian for now; the line, the column, and the ^ say where):

blocks.title: An error is a hint, not a punishment
blocks.html: Read it from the bottom up: which line, then the ^ mark points at exactly where. Most beginner errors are a bracket or a quote that was never closed.

blocks.question: What does this program print?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right. wok always moves to a new line after printing, so two calls give two lines.
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember: wok moves to a new line, wok_ does not.

blocks.question: Which function does JRG run first?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly. main is the way in, wherever it is written in the file.
blocks.feedbackNo: Try again — its position in the file does not decide the order.

blocks.html:
1. Write a program that prints your name and your age on two separate lines.

2. Change it so both appear on one line.

Answer 1: two wok calls in a row.
Answer 2: one wok("Budi", 17), or use wok_ for the first.

blocks.title: On to JRG 2
blocks.html: Now you can make the computer write. Next: making it remember — storing values in variables.

content.title: Variables & Types
content.subtitle: How the computer remembers. And one thing that trips many people up at the start: JRG tells whole numbers apart from numbers with a decimal point.

blocks.text: Storing a value under a name

blocks.html: A variable is like a labelled box. You put a value in it, then call it up by its name.

blocks.text: Three keywords, and the difference is real

rows: A value that does not change for the whole program — this is the default choice
A value that really has to change, such as a counter
A constant written outside functions, such as PI

blocks.html: This is not a formality. If you write let and then try to change it, JRG refuses — and that saves you from changing something you did not mean to.

blocks.output:
error[E0103]: `score` was declared with `let`, so it cannot be reassigned.
 --> let-refused.jrg:3:5
  |
3 |     score = 10
  |     ^^^^^
  |
  = help: use `var` or `let mut` if the value really has to change
  = note: `let` and `const` bind their value; `var` and `:=` do not

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Writing let and then wanting to change the value. Change it to var — the error message says so directly (its help: line).
The numbers 7 and 7.0 look like the same value, but JRG treats them differently. The first is a whole number (int), the second a number with a decimal point (float).

blocks.title: This is the trap that catches the most people
blocks.html: Dividing two whole numbers gives a whole number — the remainder is thrown away, not rounded. So 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5 and not 4. If you want 3.5, one of the sides has to be a float.

blocks.text: Type annotations: documentation, not a guard

blocks.html: You may write a type after a colon. JRG checks that the type name exists, but does not force the value to match — JRG is dynamically typed.

blocks.output:
error[E0103]: the type `Ghost` does not exist
 --> annotation-wrong.jrg:2:12
  |
2 |     let x: Ghost = 5
  |            ^^^^^
  |
  = help: declare `struct Ghost`/`enum Ghost`, or use a type that exists
  = note: JRG does NOT enforce type annotations — `let x: int = "text"` is accepted — so what is checked here is only whether the name EXISTS, not whether the value fits

blocks.title: So what are annotations for?
blocks.html: For the next reader — including you three months from now. They state what you meant. JRG only guards the spelling of the type name, and that is a mistake that really happens.

blocks.question: What is 9 / 2 in JRG?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly. Both are int, so the result is an int and the remainder is thrown away.
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember: int / int stays int. The remainder is thrown away, not rounded.

blocks.question: Which one gives 4.5?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right. One float side is enough to make the result a float.
blocks.feedbackNo: The third option divides first (giving 4), then converts — so 4.0.

blocks.question: When should you use var instead of let?

options.text: When the value really has to change
When the value is a number

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly. Start with let; move to var only when you need to.
blocks.feedbackNo: The other way round — let is the default choice.

blocks.html:
1. Store a price of 15000 and a quantity of 3, then print the total.

2. Work out the average of 7 and 8 so the result is 7.5, not 7.

Answer 1: let total = 15000 * 3 then wok(total).
Answer 2: (7 + 8) as float / 2.0 — written as (7+8)/2 the result is 7.

blocks.title: On to JRG 3
blocks.html: You can store things now. Next: calculating — and knowing which operators behave unexpectedly.

content.title: Operators & Arithmetic
content.subtitle: Every way to calculate in JRG, including the remainder, which turns out to be far more useful than it looks.

blocks.text: The remainder (%) is a multi-purpose tool

blocks.html: The remainder answers: “if this is shared out evenly, how much is left over?” Many tricks are born from this one operator.

blocks.output:
Even? true
Divisible by 3? true
Last digit: 8

blocks.title: Patterns worth remembering
blocks.html: n % 2 == 0 → even. n % k == 0 → divisible by k. n % 10 → the last digit. All three keep coming up in programming problems.
Just as in math: powers first, then multiply/divide, then add/subtract. Brackets beat everything.

blocks.title: Powers bind from the right
blocks.html: 2 ** 3 ** 2 means 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512, not (2**3)**2 = 64. That matches the math rule, and differs from the other operators, which bind from the left.

rows: Less / greater than or equal to

blocks.html: && means “and” (both must be true). || means “or” (one is enough). ! flips it.

blocks.output:
May enter? false
Needs checking? true

blocks.html: Writing score = score + 10 feels long. There is a short form:

blocks.code:
pub fn main() {
    var n = 10
    n += 5   
    n -= 3   
    n *= 2   
    n /= 4   
    wok(n)
}

blocks.question: What is 17 % 5?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly. 17 = 3×5 + 2, so the remainder is 2.
blocks.feedbackNo: The remainder answers what is left over, not the result of the division.

blocks.question: What is 2 + 3 * 4?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right, the multiplication goes first: 2 + 12.
blocks.feedbackNo: Multiplication and division always come before addition and subtraction.

blocks.question: How do you check that a number n is odd?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly — the remainder after dividing by 2 is always 0 or 1, and 1 means odd.
blocks.feedbackNo: Think again: what marks an odd number is the remainder.

blocks.html:
1. Print whether 91 is divisible by 7.

2. Work out 3 ** 4 without using **.

Answer 1: wok(91 % 7 == 0) → true.
Answer 2: 3 * 3 * 3 * 3 = 81, or math::pow(3, 4), which answers 81.0.

blocks.title: On to JRG 4
blocks.html: Calculating is not enough. Next: making a program choose its path based on the situation.

content.title: Branching: if & match
content.subtitle: Making a program choose a path. Two ways: one for free-form conditions, one for matching values.

blocks.title: No brackets around the condition
blocks.html: Unlike C or Java, an if condition in JRG does not need to be wrapped in brackets. What is required is the curly braces { }, even for a single line — that closes off a whole class of classic bugs.

blocks.title: Order matters
blocks.html: Branches are checked from the top. If n >= 70 were placed first, a score of 95 would stop there and get a “C”. Arrange them from the strictest condition down.
In JRG, if is not just a statement — it can be used directly as a value.

blocks.title: The short form: $
blocks.html: For a simple choice there is the compact form condition $ a : b. Read it as: “if the condition holds, take a, otherwise b”. It opens with $, not ? — in JRG the question mark is used for something else.
When you compare one value against many possibilities, match is far tidier than a pile of else if.

rows: Any value, as long as it is over 100

blocks.title: match must cover every possibility
blocks.html: If a value is caught by none of the patterns, the program stops with an error naming the value — it never quietly produces an empty value. That is what the _ on the last line is for.

blocks.question: What does if 5 > 3 { "yes" } else { "no" } give?

options.text: An error, if cannot be a value

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly — in JRG, if produces the value of the chosen branch.
blocks.feedbackNo: In JRG if can be used as a value, and what comes out is the content of its branch.

blocks.question: Why does _ go last in a match?

options.text: Because it matches anything, so the patterns below it would never be reached

blocks.feedbackOk: Right. Patterns are checked from the top, so a _ at the top would swallow everything.
blocks.feedbackNo: Think about the order of checking — top to bottom.

blocks.question: The short form of a branch in JRG opens with?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly: condition $ a : b. The ? mark is used for propagating errors.
blocks.feedbackNo: Not ? — in JRG that mark has another job.

blocks.html:
1. Write a function that takes a number and returns "positive", "negative", or "zero".

2. Rewrite that function using match.

Answer 1: three branches, if/else if/else, checking > 0 then < 0.
Answer 2: match n { 0 => "zero", x if x > 0 => "positive", _ => "negative" }.

blocks.title: On to JRG 5
blocks.html: Next come loops — and there is one thing about JRG you must know before writing your first for.

content.title: Loops
content.subtitle: Repeating work without copying code. This chapter holds one JRG-specific thing that, if you do not know it, lets your program run smoothly while answering wrong.

blocks.text: The first thing you must know about for

blocks.html: In many languages, for x in list gives you the contents of the list. In JRG, it gives you the position number (the index).

blocks.title: Why this is dangerous
blocks.html: The program above does not error. It runs, prints numbers, and exits calmly — the numbers are just wrong. If you used it to add up scores, you would get the total of 0+1+2, not of the real scores.
The form that binds the contents uses two names, separated by a comma:

blocks.output:
Item 0 holds 70
Item 1 holds 85
Item 2 holds 90

blocks.html: If you do not need the position number, write _ in its place. That mark means “it is there, but deliberately unused”.

rows: you really need the position number
this is what you want most often

blocks.text: Number ranges work the same way

blocks.html: 1..=5 makes a row of five numbers. But for n in 1..=5 still gives the index — that is, 0 to 4.

blocks.title: The one-sentence rule
blocks.html: If there is only one name after for, it always holds the position number — for arrays, strings, and ranges alike. Need the contents? Use two names.

blocks.text: while — as long as the condition holds

blocks.html: Use while when you do not know how many times to repeat, only when to stop.

blocks.title: A loop that never stops
blocks.html: If a while condition never becomes false, your program hangs forever. Make sure something inside the body moves you toward the stopping condition — in the example above, left shrinks on every round.

rows: Skip the rest of the body, go on to the next round

blocks.question: What does for x in [10, 20, 30] { wok_(x, " ") } print?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly — one name means the index. This is the JRG trap that catches the most people.
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember the rule: one name after for always holds the position number.

blocks.question: How do you add up the contents of an array a?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right. _ throws the index away, x receives the value.
blocks.feedbackNo: The first option adds up the indices (0+1+2+…), not the contents — and nothing tells you.

blocks.question: What is the difference between break and continue?

options.text: break leaves the loop, continue jumps to the next round

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly.
blocks.feedbackNo: break stops; continue skips only the rest of this round's body.

blocks.html:
1. Print all the even numbers from 1 to 20.

2. Count how many numbers in [3, 8, 12, 5, 20] are greater than 6.

3. Print the 7 times table (7×1 to 7×10).

Answer 1: for _, n in 1..=20 { if n % 2 == 0 { wok_(n, " ") } }
Answer 2: use a counter var c = 0, then for _, n in a { if n > 6 { c += 1 } } → 3.
Answer 3: for _, i in 1..=10 { wok("7 x", i, "=", 7 * i) }

blocks.title: On to JRG 6
blocks.html: You can repeat things now. Next: wrapping work up as a function, so it can be used many times without being copied.

content.title: Functions
content.subtitle: Giving a name to a piece of work, so it can be called again and again without copying a single line.

rows: The keyword that opens a function
The name — ideally a verb, or a description of the result
The parameter: the value received from the caller
The type of the value returned

blocks.title: Why split things into functions?
blocks.html: Three reasons: no copying code, the function's name explains the intent, and when the formula changes you only fix one place.
A parameter may have a fallback value. If the caller does not fill it in, that value is used.
Not every function produces a value. Some only do something — printing, for example.
A function may call other functions, including itself. That last one is called recursion.

blocks.title: Recursion needs a brake
blocks.html: The line if n <= 1 { return 1 } is the brake. Without a stopping condition, the function keeps calling itself until JRG stops it and reports the call depth — it never goes quiet.

blocks.text: The order you write them in does not matter

blocks.html: A function may be called before the line that declares it. JRG reads the whole file first, then runs main.

blocks.text: Type annotations do not force anything

blocks.html: As in JRG 2: the type name is checked, the value is not. A function marked float still accepts an int.

blocks.question: What is return for?

options.text: Handing a value back to the caller and leaving the function

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly — and it also ends the function, so the lines below it are not run.
blocks.feedbackNo: return prints nothing; wok is what prints.

blocks.question: Why does a recursive function need a stopping condition?

options.text: So it can be called from main

blocks.feedbackOk: Right. Without one, the calls pile up until the depth limit is reached.
blocks.feedbackNo: Think about what happens if the function always calls itself.

blocks.question: Can a function be called on a line before it is written?

options.text: No, it has to be written first
Yes — JRG reads the whole file first

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly.
blocks.feedbackNo: Try running the 'fn-order.jrg' example above — it runs normally.

blocks.html:
1. Make a function cube(n) that returns n³.

2. Make a function maximum(a, b) without using math::max.

3. Make a recursive function that adds up 1 to n.

Answer 1: return n * n * n, or return n ** 3.
Answer 2: if a > b { return a } then return b.
Answer 3: if n <= 0 { return 0 } then return n + sum(n - 1).

blocks.title: On to JRG 7
blocks.html: Next: storing many values at once with arrays, and working with text.

content.title: Arrays & Text
content.subtitle: Keeping many values under one name, and working with sentences. The two types you will use most after numbers.

blocks.code:
pub fn main() {
    let scores = [70, 85, 90, 65]
    wok(scores)
    wok("How many:", len(scores))
    wok("The first:", scores[0])
    wok("The last:", scores[len(scores) - 1])
}
blocks.output:
[70, 85, 90, 65]
How many: 4
The first: 70
The last: 65

blocks.title: Counting starts at zero
blocks.html: The first element is at position 0, not 1. So an array of 4 elements has positions 0, 1, 2, 3 — and scores[4] is an error.
JRG has a shortcut for positions counted from the end: negative numbers.

blocks.output:
error: index [5] is out of bounds — this array holds 2 elements (valid indices: 0..1, or -1..-2 counting from the end)
 --> out-of-range.jrg:3:9
  |
3 |     wok(a[5])
  |         ^^^^
  |

blocks.title: Out of range is always an error
blocks.html: JRG never quietly returns an empty value for a position that does not exist. It stops and states the real length ("isinya 2 elemen" — it holds 2 elements) — far better than a program that carries on with a fake value.

rows: an int if the contents are ints
the old one does not change

blocks.code:
pub fn main() {
    let n = [8, 3, 10, 1]
    wok("Sum     :", arr::sum(n))
    wok("Average :", arr::mean(n))
    wok("Largest :", arr::max(n))
    wok("Sorted  :", arr::sort(n))
    wok("Original:", n)
}

blocks.title: An array never changes behind your back
blocks.html: Look at the last line: after arr::sort, n is still as it was. In JRG every value is owned by one name; functions give a new array. To keep the result, assign it back: n = arr::sort(n).

blocks.code:
pub fn main() {
    let s = "Learning JRG"
    wok("Length      :", len(s))
    wok("Upper case  :", str::upper(s))
    wok("Has 'JRG'?  :", str::contains(s, "JRG"))
    wok("Replace     :", str::replace(s, "JRG", "math"))
}
blocks.output:
Length      : 12
Upper case  : LEARNING JRG
Has 'JRG'?  : true
Replace     : Learning math

blocks.html: Joining text uses +. If one side is a number, the number is turned into text.
Each {} is filled in order by the values after it. To limit the digits after the decimal point, use {:.N}.

blocks.title: When to use {:.2}
blocks.html: Whenever you show money, report-card scores, or measurements. Without it, 1/3 shows up as 0.3333333333333333 — correct, but not pleasant to read.

blocks.output:
[sari, budi, tono]
There are 3 names
sari & budi & tono

blocks.question: The position of the first element of an array is?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly. The first element is at position 0.
blocks.feedbackNo: In JRG (as in most languages) counting starts from zero.

blocks.question: After arr::sort(n), is n itself sorted?

options.text: No — the result is a new array

blocks.feedbackOk: Right. Keep the result if you need it: n = arr::sort(n).
blocks.feedbackNo: Run the arr.jrg example above and look at its last line.

blocks.question: What does str::format("{:.1}", 3.456) give?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly — one digit after the decimal point, and the value is rounded.
blocks.feedbackNo: {:.1} rounds to one digit after the decimal point.

blocks.html:
1. From [12, 7, 25, 3], print the difference between the largest and the smallest.

2. Count the letters in the sentence "I learn JRG" without counting spaces.

Answer 1: arr::max(a) - arr::min(a) → 22.
Answer 2: len(str::replace(s, " ", "")) → 9.

blocks.title: On to JRG 8
blocks.html: Next: making your own data type with struct, so values that belong together do not wander around separately.

content.title: Structs & Methods
content.subtitle: Making your own data type. So that a "point" is no longer two variables that happen to sit next to each other, but one whole thing.

blocks.html: Imagine you store a student's data: name, score, and attendance. Without a struct, the three become separate variables — and nothing ties them together.
Now imagine there are 30 students. A struct solves that:

blocks.text: pub: fields that may be seen from outside

blocks.html: Notice the word pub in front of each field. Without it, a field can only be read from inside that type's own methods — and JRG refuses if you try to read it from outside.

blocks.output:
error: the field `balance` of `Wallet` is private — it can only be reached from inside that type's own methods or its descendants'. Add `pub` in front of the field in the struct declaration if it really has to be public.
 --> private.jrg:7:9
  |
7 |     wok(w.balance)
  |         ^^^^^^^^^
  |

blocks.title: This is not a hassle, it is a choice
blocks.html: A closed field forces data to change only through methods you write yourself — so the rule (say, "the balance can never go negative") lives in one place, not scattered over every line that touches it.

blocks.text: Methods: functions that belong to a type

blocks.html: An impl block attaches functions to a struct. Inside it, self means “the thing being called”.

blocks.title: Why a method, not a plain function?
blocks.html: Because the rule belongs to that type. a.passed() reads more clearly than passed(a), and if another type with different rules appears later, the two do not get in each other's way.
A method without self is called through the type's name. It is usually used to build the starting value.

blocks.output:
Settings {height: 24, title: Untitled, width: 80}
Settings {height: 24, title: Report, width: 80}

blocks.html: If you copy a struct to another name, the two stand on their own. Changing one never touches the other — this is a core JRG rule.

blocks.title: Why this is a relief
blocks.html: In many languages, handing an object to another function means that function can change yours. Not in JRG. You never have to guess who is quietly changing your data.

blocks.text: Showing a struct your own way

blocks.html: If a type has a method named to_string, every place that prints will use it.

blocks.question: What does self mean inside an impl block?

options.text: The thing whose method is being called

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly. If you call a.passed(), then self is a.
blocks.feedbackNo: Think of a.passed() — who is self there?

blocks.question: After var b = a and then b.item = 99, what is a.item?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right. In JRG assignment makes a copy; two names never share contents.
blocks.feedbackNo: The core JRG rule: values never share a place.

blocks.question: How do you call a method that has no self?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly — through the type's name, using ::.
blocks.feedbackNo: Without self it is not tied to a particular thing, so it is called through the type's name.

blocks.html:
1. Make a struct Square with a field side, and methods area() and perimeter().

2. Add a method biggerThan(other) that answers true/false.

Answer 1: fn area(self) -> int { return self.side * self.side }, perimeter 4 * self.side.
Answer 2: fn biggerThan(self, other: Square) -> bool { return self.area() > other.area() }.

blocks.title: On to JRG 9
blocks.html: Next: treating functions as values — handed over, stored, and run later.

content.title: Functions as Values
content.subtitle: In JRG a function is not just something you call — it can be stored in a variable, handed to another function, and made on the spot.

blocks.text: Storing a function in a variable

blocks.html: If a function is only used once, it does not need a name. The short form uses a pair of vertical bars.

blocks.title: Why it is called a closure
blocks.html: Because it "closes over" the values around it — variables from outside stay readable inside it, even after that line has passed.

blocks.text: Three functions that change how you write

rows: Keep the ones that meet a condition
Squeeze it down to one value

blocks.html: Compare it with writing a loop — both are correct, but the one above states what you want, not how to do it.

blocks.output:
With a loop  : [12, 18]
With a filter: [12, 18]

blocks.html: You can write your own functions that take a function as a parameter.

blocks.question: What does arr::map([1,2,3], |x| x * 10) give?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly — map changes every element and gives a new array as long as the original.
blocks.feedbackNo: map does not add things up; reduce does.

blocks.question: Which function squeezes an array down to one value?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right.
blocks.feedbackNo: map and filter both give an array.

blocks.html:
1. From [3, 8, 15, 4, 22], take the ones greater than 5 and multiply them by 2.

2. Find the product of everything in [1, 2, 3, 4] using reduce.

Answer 1: arr::map(arr::filter(a, |x| x > 5), |x| x * 2) → [16, 30, 44].
Answer 2: arr::reduce(a, |x, y| x * y, 1) → 24. Note that the starting value is 1, not 0.

blocks.title: On to JRG 10
blocks.html: Next: what JRG does when an answer might not exist — and why that is not nil.

content.title: When the Answer Might Not Exist
content.subtitle: How JRG handles "not found" and "failed" — without ever handing over a fake value that looks like an answer.

blocks.html: What should a search function return when the thing it looks for is not there? Many languages answer null — and that is where the trouble starts, because null looks like an ordinary value until the program has already used it.
JRG answers differently: such a function returns an Option, which holds one of two things — Some(value) if it was found, or None if it was not.

blocks.title: The short form: ??
blocks.html: a ?? b means "use a if it has a value, otherwise use b". The difference from unwrap_or: b is only computed when it is actually needed.

blocks.text: Result: success, or failure with a reason

blocks.html: When a failure has a cause that needs explaining, JRG uses Result: Ok(value) or Err(reason).

blocks.output:
Result: 5
Failed: cannot divide by zero

blocks.html: Writing a match for every call is tiring. The ? mark means: "if this failed, stop this function and pass the error upward".

blocks.title: This is why ? does not open a branch
blocks.html: In JRG the question mark already has this job — passing errors on. That is why the short form of a branch uses $, not ? as in other languages.
If a function may answer nil for "not found", then nil has two meanings: “not there” and “there, but empty”. Two different situations with the same answer — and the program cannot tell them apart.

lines.html: Some(nil) → there is a value, it happens to be empty

blocks.question: What does [1,2].get(99) return?

options.text: An error that stops the program

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly — None, which you have to open before using.
blocks.feedbackNo: JRG uses Option for things that might not be found.

blocks.question: What does ? at the end of a function call mean?

options.text: The short form of a branch
If it failed, stop this function and pass the error on

blocks.feedbackOk: Right.
blocks.feedbackNo: The short form of a branch in JRG is $.

blocks.question: Why is None better than nil for "not found"?

options.text: Because nil would have two meanings at once

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly — and two meanings in one answer is a source of bugs that are hard to track down.
blocks.feedbackNo: Think: what happens when the value stored really is nil?

blocks.html:
1. Write a function root(n) that refuses negative numbers using Result.

2. Take element 5 of an array with 3 elements, with a fallback of 0.

Answer 1: if n < 0 { return Err("square root of a negative number") } then return Ok(math::sqrt(n)).
Answer 2: a.get(5).unwrap_or(0), or a.get(5) ?? 0.

blocks.title: On to JRG 11
blocks.html: Next: storing paired data — a name and its value — with a dict.

content.title: Dicts: Paired Data
content.subtitle: Storing data that is looked up by name, not by position. Like a dictionary: you look up a word, you get its meaning.

blocks.text: When an array is not enough

blocks.html: Arrays are good for ordered lists. But if you want to store a value per name — Sari's score, Budi's score — a position number does not help.

blocks.title: dict::get answers an Option
blocks.html: Just like a.get(i) on an array: if the key is not there, the answer is None — not a zero pretending to be a real value.
As with arrays, the two-name form gives the key and its value.

blocks.title: The order is always the same
blocks.html: A dict is printed and walked in a fixed key order, so your program's output does not change from run to run. That matters when you compare the result or save it to a file.
Whatever you use as a key is stored as its written form. So d[0] and d["0"] point at the same place.

rows: An array of all the keys
An array of all the values

blocks.question: When is a dict a better fit than an array?

options.text: When there is a lot of data
When data is looked up by name, not by position

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly.
blocks.feedbackNo: What makes the difference is not the amount of data, but how you look it up.

blocks.question: What does dict::get(d, "missing") give?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right — just like a.get(i) on an array.
blocks.feedbackNo: JRG uses Option for things that might not be found.

blocks.html:
1. Make a dict of the prices of three items, then print the total price.

2. Find the most expensive item in that dict.

Answer 1: arr::sum(dict::values(d)).
Answer 2: walk it with for name, p in d while keeping the largest, or arr::max(dict::values(d)) if you do not need the item's name.

blocks.title: On to JRG 12
blocks.html: The last chapter: reading error messages — the skill that makes you independent fastest.

content.title: Reading Error Messages
content.subtitle: The skill that makes you independent fastest. Every message in this chapter comes straight from JRG — none of them is rewritten. JRG's messages are in Indonesian for now (English messages are on the way), so each one is explained in English underneath.

blocks.text: An error is not a sign that you failed

blocks.html: Error messages are the one part of a programming language that really teaches. They know exactly what is wrong and where. All you need to do is read them to the end — most people stop at the first line.
Every JRG error has four parts:

rows: What is wrong, in everyday words
A piece of your code, with a pointer right underneath
A suggested fix, when JRG has one

blocks.output:
error: the variable `totl` is not known — did you mean `total`? if not, check the spelling, or maybe you forgot `let totl = ...` first
 --> typo.jrg:3:9
  |
3 |     wok(totl)
  |         ^^^^
  |

blocks.title: JRG guesses what you meant
blocks.html: Look for the part that names a similar name (maksudnya `total`? — “did you mean `total`?”). If a name is only one letter off, JRG suggests it — so you do not have to check every name one by one.

blocks.text: A bracket that was never closed

blocks.title: The line pointed at is not always the line that is wrong
blocks.html: Here the pointer is on the } of line 3 (“there should be a ) here, but a } was found”), while what is missing is the ) on line 2. That is natural: JRG only notices something is missing when it finds a mark that does not fit. If the pointer is on a closing bracket, check the line above it.

blocks.output:
error: index [7] is out of bounds — this array holds 3 elements (valid indices: 0..2, or -1..-3 counting from the end)
 --> oob.jrg:3:9
  |
3 |     wok(a[7])
  |         ^^^^
  |

blocks.html: Notice that the message states the real length (“this array holds 3 elements, valid indices 0..2”). That usually tells you the cause right away: a counter that is one too high, or data that is shorter than you expected.

blocks.text: Changing a value that may not change

blocks.output:
error[E0103]: `limit` was declared with `let`, so it cannot be reassigned.
 --> let-error.jrg:3:5
  |
3 |     limit = 200
  |     ^^^^^
  |
  = help: use `var` or `let mut` if the value really has to change
  = note: `let` and `const` bind their value; `var` and `:=` do not

blocks.html: “limit was declared with let, so it cannot be reassigned”, and the help: line says to use var or let mut if the value really has to change.

blocks.text: Types that do not fit together

blocks.output:
error: cannot `%` between `int` and `string`
 --> type-error.jrg:2:9
  |
2 |     wok(5 % "two")
  |         ^^^^^^^^^
  |

blocks.title: The message names the types, not the contents
blocks.html: JRG deliberately writes int and string (“cannot % between int and string”), not the values you passed. If your data held ten thousand numbers, printing them would drown the message itself.
Some errors only show up once the program is running — for example a division by zero whose numbers are only known later. JRG lists the chain of calls that led there.

blocks.output:
error: `100 / 0` — cannot divide by zero, the result is never defined. Check the divisor before dividing
 --> chain.jrg:2:12
  |
2 |     return a / b
  |            ^^^^^
  |
  = trace: `divide` called at chain.jrg:6:12
           `average` called at chain.jrg:10:9

blocks.title: Read the chain from the bottom up
blocks.html: The trace: lines say who called whom. The bottom line is where you started, the top is where the error happened. What often needs fixing is the one at the bottom — that is where the wrong value came from.

blocks.text: Three steps when you are stuck

lines.html: 1. Read the whole message, including the help: line
2. Narrow down — delete half the code until the error disappears; what you removed last is the cause
3. Try it with the Edit and Run buttons on any example on this page

blocks.question: If the ^ pointer is on a }, where is the mistake usually?

options.text: On a line before it — something was not closed

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly. JRG only notices something is missing when it finds a mark that does not fit.
blocks.feedbackNo: Think about when JRG can know that a bracket is missing.

blocks.question: Why does an error message name the type, not the contents of the data?

options.text: So it stays short and does not grow with the size of the data
Because JRG does not know the contents

blocks.feedbackOk: Right — a message that grows with the data would drown its own explanation.
blocks.feedbackNo: Imagine an error message for an array of ten thousand numbers.

blocks.question: The most powerful step when you cannot find the cause of an error?

options.text: Deleting half the code until the error disappears

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly — this is called bisection, and it works for almost every bug.
blocks.feedbackNo: What you want is a way to narrow it down, not to change things.

blocks.html:
1. Write a deliberately wrong program, and guess which error will appear before running it.

2. Take one error message from this chapter, and point out which line has to be fixed.

Hint: guessing before running is the best exercise — if your guess is off, you have just found something you do not understand yet.

blocks.title: The JRG path is done
blocks.html: You have been through all of it: writing, storing, calculating, choosing, repeating, wrapping work in functions, making your own types, and reading errors. The math path next to it will now feel much easier — each of its chapters uses what you just learned.

content.title: Numbers
content.subtitle: Before calculating anything, we need to agree on what a number is, and how many "kinds" of number there are. This chapter is the foundation — understand it well here, and the following chapters get much lighter.

blocks.html: Every number you have ever written belongs to one of the following "families". The further down the table, the bigger the family — each family contains the families above it.

rows: Can be written as a fraction a/b
Decimals that never repeat & never end
All of the above together — every point on the number line

blocks.title: Why group them?
blocks.html: Because different families follow different rules. Dividing two integers does not always give an integer (7 ÷ 2 = 3.5), but dividing two natural numbers with a remainder of zero always does. Knowing the "kind" of number you hold helps you guess the kind of answer.
The easiest way to picture integers is as equally spaced points on a line. Zero in the middle, positives to the right, negatives to the left.

−4
−3
−2
−1
0
1
2
3
4
The further right, the bigger the value — not the "more digits". This matters: −1 is bigger than −100, even though "100" looks bigger than "1".
The number 2507 is really shorthand for a sum based on the position of each digit:

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Thinking the "0" is unimportant and can be dropped. But 2507 and 257 are different numbers — the zero holds the other digits in place.

1. Which families does −7 belong to? (more than one is allowed)

2. Between −15 and −3, which is bigger? Why?

Answer 1: Integer (ℤ), Rational (ℚ), and Real (ℝ) — but not Natural/Whole, because it is negative.
Answer 2: −3 is bigger. On the number line, −3 is to the right of −15, closer to zero.
In programming, these "kinds of number" have their own technical name: data types. JRG has two main number types — int for integers, and float for numbers with a decimal point.

blocks.output:
Age: 17
Height: 165.5 cm
Zero is still a number: 0

blocks.title: Why separate int and float?
blocks.html: The computer stores them differently in memory. An int is more compact and exact, but cannot hold a decimal point. Type annotations in JRG are only documentation: let x: int = 3.5 is still accepted, and x stays 3.5, a float. Only the existence of the type name is checked (see JRG 2).

blocks.question: Which group does −8 belong to?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! −8 has no decimal point and can be negative, so it is an Integer (ℤ), not a Natural/Whole number, which are always positive-or-zero.
blocks.feedbackNo: Try again — remember, Natural & Whole numbers are never negative.

blocks.question: Which is bigger: −20 or −5?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right! On the number line, the further right, the bigger. −5 is to the right of −20.
blocks.feedbackNo: Not quite. Picture the number line — which one is further right?

blocks.question: The code let x: int = 7.2 in JRG will...

options.text: Succeed — annotations are not enforced, x stays 7.2 (a float)

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! Type annotations in JRG are only documentation. JRG checks that the name int exists, but does not force the value to match — so typeof(x) is still float.
blocks.feedbackNo: Not quite. Try running let x: int = 7.2 then wok(x, typeof(x)) — JRG is dynamically typed (see JRG 2).

blocks.title: On to Chapter 2
blocks.html: Now you know the kinds of number. Next: how these numbers interact through addition and subtraction — including tricks for quick mental arithmetic.

content.title: Addition & Subtraction
content.subtitle: The two most basic operations — but with properties that, once mastered, make mental arithmetic much faster than relying on a calculator.

blocks.title: What associativity buys you
blocks.html: When adding many numbers, you are free to group the easy ones first. Adding 28 + 47 + 2? Group 28 + 2 first (=30), then 30 + 47 = 77. Much faster than going left to right.
The most important idea in this chapter: a − b is the same as a + (−b). That is why subtraction is not commutative and not associative — you are really adding numbers whose signs depend on the order.

blocks.text: A quick-arithmetic trick: rounding to the tens

blocks.html: For something like 47 + 38, do not calculate it as it stands. Round one number to the nearest ten first, then correct:

blocks.title: A common mistake in word problems
blocks.html: "Andi has 10 apples and gives 4 to a friend" → many students write 4 − 10 because of the order of the numbers in the sentence. The right way: find the starting amount (10) minus the amount lost (4) → 10 − 4 = 6. The order in a word problem ≠ the order in the formula.

1. Calculate quickly: 96 + 27 (use the rounding trick).

2. The morning temperature is −3°C, and it rises 12°C by noon. What is the noon temperature?

Answer 1: 96 + 27 = 96 + 30 − 3 = 126 − 3 = 123
Answer 2: −3 + 12 = 9°C

blocks.text: Variables that change: mut and the short operators

blocks.html: In JRG, an ordinary variable (let) cannot change its value once defined. For a variable whose value will change — like a balance or a score — you must mark it mut (mutable), or declare it with var.

blocks.code:
pub fn main() {
    let mut balance = 50000
    wok("Starting balance:", balance)

    balance += 20000  // same as balance = balance + 20000
    wok("After saving:", balance)

    balance -= 35000  // same as balance = balance - 35000
    wok("After shopping:", balance)
}
blocks.output:
Starting balance: 50000
After saving: 70000
After shopping: 35000

blocks.title: If you forget mut
blocks.html: Writing balance += 20000 on a variable declared with plain let makes JRG refuse the program before it runs — the error says that `balance` was declared with `let`, so it cannot be reassigned, and suggests var. This is not a bug, it is a safety feature, so you do not accidentally change a value that should stay fixed.

blocks.question: Which one is TRUE about subtraction?

options.text: The order of subtraction does not matter

blocks.feedbackOk: Right! 8−3=5 but 3−8=−5, the results have different signs. The order matters a lot.
blocks.feedbackNo: Work out 8−3 and 3−8 — are the results the same?

blocks.question: A quick way to calculate 59 + 34 is...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! 34 is rounded up to 40 (6 too many), so take 6 off at the end: 99−6=93.
blocks.feedbackNo: Check the rounding again — 59+34 must still equal 93.

blocks.question: In JRG, a variable whose value will change must be marked...
blocks.feedbackOk: Right, let mut marks a variable whose value may change (so does var).
blocks.feedbackNo: Not quite — const is for values that may NOT change at all.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 3
blocks.html: Once addition and subtraction are smooth, it is the turn of multiplication and division — including the idea of a "remainder", which is very important in programming.

content.title: Multiplication & Division
content.subtitle: Multiplication is "repeated addition, sped up". Division hides one idea that is used constantly in programming: the remainder.

lines.html: "4 groups of 3" or "3 groups of 4" — the result is always the same (commutative)

blocks.html: Like addition, multiplication is commutative (a×b=b×a), associative ((a×b)×c=a×(b×c)), and has an identity — but the identity is 1, not 0, because a × 1 = a.

blocks.title: The times-9 trick
blocks.html: For 9 × n (n = 1 to 10): the answer is always (n−1) in front, then (10−n) behind. For example 9×7: front = 6, back = 3 → 63. Try 9×4: front=3, back=6 → 36. ✓
When 17 is divided by 5, the result is not a tidy whole number. There are two ways to look at it:

The remainder (modulo) is "what is left over" after sharing out evenly as much as possible. It is an idea you will use again and again — to check even/odd, to take turns, to work with clocks (24 hours repeating), and much more.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Dividing by zero. Mathematically, a ÷ 0 is undefined — not "infinity", not "zero", it really has no answer. A program that tries it usually crashes or raises an error, rather than quietly giving a strange result.

1. What are the quotient and the remainder of 29 ÷ 6?

2. Is 234 even? How do you check with modulo?

Answer 1: Quotient = 4, remainder = 5 (because 6×4=24, 29−24=5)
Answer 2: Even. 234 mod 2 = 0 → if the remainder after dividing by 2 is 0, it is even.

blocks.text: The % operator for checking even and odd

blocks.html: In JRG (as in most programming languages), the modulo symbol is %. It is one of the most used operators — far more often than it looks in a math class.

blocks.title: Where else is it used?
blocks.html: An analogue clock "goes round" every 12 — that is modulo 12. A game grid that "wraps around" to the other side — that is modulo the grid width. Sharing turns evenly between players — modulo the number of players. Once you get it, you will see it everywhere.

blocks.question: What is 22 mod 7?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! 7×3=21, so what is left is 22−21=1.
blocks.feedbackNo: Try again — how many times does 7 go into 22, and what is left?

blocks.question: Why can 9 × 6 = 54 be worked out quickly as "5, 4"?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right, that is the times-9 trick pattern, which holds for 1–10.
blocks.feedbackNo: Look again at the formula in the times-9 trick above.

blocks.question: What happens if we divide by 0?

options.text: It is undefined / a program usually errors

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! Division by zero has no valid mathematical answer.
blocks.feedbackNo: Not quite — read the "A common mistake" box above again.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 4
blocks.html: If a single problem has addition, subtraction, multiplication, AND division all at once — which goes first? That is the next chapter: the order of operations.

content.title: Order of Operations
content.subtitle: When one problem has addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and brackets all at once — the math world has agreed on the order to work them out. Without this rule, one problem could have several conflicting "right answers".

blocks.html: These two acronyms teach the same order, with different words:

rows: Multiplication & Division (left to right, equal rank)
Addition & Subtraction (left to right, equal rank)

blocks.title: Common mistake #1
blocks.html: Multiplication & division have equal rank — they go from left to right, not "multiplication always first". The same goes for addition & subtraction. So 20 ÷ 4 × 2 = (20÷4)×2 = 10, not 20÷(4×2)=2.5.

blocks.title: Common mistake #2
blocks.html: Working left to right regardless of the kind of operation (8+2=10 first, then ×2... and so on). That gives a completely wrong answer. The order of kinds of operation always beats the order of where they are written.

1. Work out: 3 + 4 × 2

2. Work out: (3 + 4) × 2

3. Work out: 10 − 2² + 1

Answer 1: 3+8 = 11 (multiply first)
Answer 2: 7×2 = 14 (brackets first, which changes the total)
Answer 3: 10−4+1 = 7 (power first, then subtract & add left to right)

blocks.text: JRG follows exactly the same rule

blocks.html: Programming-language compilers and interpreters, JRG included, evaluate expressions with operator precedence rules that copy ordinary math. Brackets are still the safest way to make sure the order is what you mean.

blocks.title: A good programmer's habit
blocks.html: Even when it is not required, many programmers add extra brackets to complicated expressions — not because they are needed, but so others (or themselves six months later) can understand the order right away without memorising a precedence table.

blocks.question: What is 6 + 3 × 4?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! 3×4=12 first, then 6+12=18.
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember, multiplication goes before addition.

blocks.question: What is (6 + 3) × 4?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right! The brackets force 6+3=9 first, then 9×4=36.
blocks.feedbackNo: Try again — brackets always go first.

blocks.question: 20 ÷ 5 × 2 equals...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! Multiplication & division have equal rank, so they go in order from the left: 20÷5=4, then 4×2=8.
blocks.feedbackNo: Not quite — multiplication and division have the SAME priority, and go from left to right.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 5
blocks.html: The order of operations is safe now. Next we look deeper at negative numbers — when a product or quotient turns negative, and the sign rules that often get mixed up.

content.title: Negative Numbers
content.subtitle: Negative numbers are not just "numbers taken away". They have their own sign rules when multiplied or divided — rules that are often remembered wrong when only memorised, not understood.

blocks.html: The easiest way to remember: same signs → positive, different signs → negative. The same rule holds for division.

blocks.title: The "enemy of my enemy is my friend" analogy
blocks.html: Negative is the "opposite/enemy" of positive. Opposing once (multiplying by a negative) turns something into its opposite. Opposing twice (negative × negative) turns it back into a friend — that is why the result is positive.
The absolute value, written |x|, is a number's distance from zero — and a distance is always positive (or zero), never negative.

lines.html: −7 and 7 are both 7 steps away from zero

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Reading −7 < |−7| as "−7 is smaller than itself". But |−7|=7, so what is compared is −7 < 7 — which is true, not strange. The absolute value turns a number into another (positive) number; it does not just "rub out the minus in place".

1. Work out: (−6) × (−7)

2. Work out: (−36) ÷ 4

3. It is 30°C in Jakarta and −5°C on a mountain top. What is the difference?

Answer 1: 42 (negative × negative = positive)
Answer 2: −9 (negative ÷ positive = negative)
Answer 3: 30 − (−5) = 35°C

Almost every programming language has a built-in absolute-value function, because the need for "how far, regardless of direction" is very common — for example the difference between two temperatures, the distance between points, or the error in a measurement.

blocks.title: In the real world
blocks.html: A bank balance can be negative (debt/credit), the depth of the sea is written as negative from sea level, and scores can drop below zero in many games. Every time you see a "−" in front of a number in an app, the rules of this chapter are at work behind it.

blocks.question: What is (−8) × (−2)?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! Negative × Negative = Positive.
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember the sign rule: a negative times a negative is positive.

blocks.question: What is |−15|?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right, the absolute value always gives a positive number (the distance from zero).
blocks.feedbackNo: Not quite — an absolute value is never negative.

blocks.question: (−24) ÷ (−6) equals...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! The same signs (negative ÷ negative) give a positive.
blocks.feedbackNo: Try again — check the sign-rule table above.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 6
blocks.html: Time for fractions and decimals — two different ways of writing numbers "between" the integers, and how to change from one form to the other.

content.title: Fractions & Decimals
content.subtitle: Fractions and decimals are two different "languages" for the same thing: part of a whole. Knowing how to move between them makes many problems much more flexible.

blocks.html: The fraction 34 is read "three quarters" — something split into 4 equal parts (the denominator), of which we take 3 (the numerator).

blocks.title: Simplifying a fraction
blocks.html: The fraction 812 can be simplified by dividing the numerator & denominator by their GCD (the GCD of 8 and 12 is 4) → giving 23. The GCD is covered in more detail in Chapter 10.

blocks.text: From fraction to decimal, and back

lines.html: Fraction → decimal: divide the numerator by the denominator
Decimal → fraction: write it over 10/100/1000, then simplify

blocks.html: This is the part most often done wrong: fractions can ONLY be added directly when their denominators are the same. If they differ, make the denominators equal first (using the LCM).

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Adding the numerators and the denominators directly: 1/2 + 1/3 ≠ 2/5. This is WRONG — a fraction is not an ordinary pair of numbers; it stands for a single value whose base (the denominator) has to be made equal before combining.

1. Turn 5/8 into a decimal.

2. Simplify the fraction 18/24.

3. Work out: 2/3 + 1/6

Answer 1: 5÷8 = 0.625
Answer 2: GCD(18,24)=6 → 3/4
Answer 3: 4/6 + 1/6 = 5/6

A computer stores a float with limited precision, so the result of a division often needs rounding to display neatly. JRG provides math::round(), math::floor() (always down), and math::ceil() (always up).

blocks.code:
pub fn main() {
    let fraction = 5.0 / 8.0
    wok("5/8 as a decimal:", fraction)

    wok("round:", math::round(0.625), "→ as int:", math::round(0.625) as int)
    wok("floor:", math::floor(0.625) as int)
    wok("ceil:", math::ceil(0.625) as int)
}
blocks.output:
5/8 as a decimal: 0.625
round: 1.0 → as int: 1
floor: 0
ceil: 1

blocks.title: A famous float trap
blocks.html: Try 0.1 + 0.2 in many programming languages — the result is often 0.30000000000000004, not a tidy 0.3! That is because decimals are stored in binary, and not every decimal fraction can be represented exactly. For money and precise calculations, many real systems use integers (for example, storing amounts in "cents" rather than decimal dollars).

blocks.question: 3/5 as a decimal is...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6
blocks.feedbackNo: Try dividing directly: 3 ÷ 5 = ?

blocks.question: 1/4 + 1/4 equals...
blocks.feedbackOk: Right! 2/4 simplified (dividing by the GCD=2) is 1/2.
blocks.feedbackNo: 2/8 gets the denominator wrong — the denominators are already equal (4), so just add the numerators.

blocks.question: Which function ALWAYS rounds down?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! floor() always goes down, ceil() always up, round() to the nearest.
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember: "floor" is below you, "ceiling" is above you.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 7
blocks.html: A percentage is really just a fraction over 100 with a special name. The next chapter ties it all together with the discounts, taxes, and interest you meet every day.

content.title: Percentages (%)
content.subtitle: "Percent" comes from the Latin per centum, meaning "per hundred". Once you remember that, percentages stop being a scary topic and become just a fraction over 100.

blocks.html: 25%, 0.25, and 1/4 are exactly the same number, just written in three different forms.

blocks.title: The key to taking a percentage of a number

lines.html: The price after a 20% discount on $150
The quick way: final price = price × (100%−20%) = 150 × 0.8 = $120

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: "Up 50%, then down 50%" does NOT bring you back to where you started! $100 up 50% → $150. $150 down 50% → $75, not $100. The reason: the second percentage is taken from a different base (from 150, not from 100 again).

1. A $200 shirt is 15% off. What is the final price?

2. A shop raises a price from $40 to $50. What is the percentage increase?

Answer 1: 200 × 0.85 = $170
Answer 2: (50−40)/40×100% = 25%

blocks.title: Why make it a function?
blocks.html: Because the formula "price × (1 − discount/100)" will be used again and again for many products. Writing it once as the function priceAfterDiscount() means no copy-pasting the same formula dozens of times — you just call the function.

blocks.question: An $80 shirt has a 25% discount. The final price?
blocks.feedbackNo: Try: discount = 25%×80=20, then 80−20.

blocks.question: A price goes up 50%, then down 50%. Compared with the starting price, the result is?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! For example 100→150→75. The base of the percentage changes at each step.
blocks.feedbackNo: Try it with an example, say starting from $100.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 8
blocks.html: So far every number has had a known value. The next chapter introduces variables — letters that stand for a number that is not (or deliberately not yet) known, and how to find it with an equation.

content.title: Variables & Equations
content.subtitle: A variable is an "empty box" standing for a number that is not known yet. An equation is a puzzle that gives you enough information to find what is in the box.

blocks.html: In x + 5 = 12, the letter x is a variable — an empty slot whose value is not known yet, but can be found because there is a rule (the equation) linking it to other numbers.

blocks.title: The golden rule of equations
blocks.html: Whatever you do to one side of an equation (add, subtract, multiply, divide), you must do exactly the same to the other side. That keeps the "scales" balanced.

blocks.text: Solving an equation step by step

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Moving a number to the other side without changing its sign. 3x + 7 = 22 does not become 3x = 22 + 7 — the right one is 3x = 22 − 7, because the "+7" that moves becomes "−7" (the same as subtracting 7 from both sides).
Sometimes one equation is not enough because two things are unknown. The way out: find two equations, then combine them by substitution.

blocks.title: When is it used?
blocks.html: A problem like "2 pencils + 1 book cost $13, and 1 pencil + 2 books cost $11; what does each cost?" is a system of two equations. Very common in secondary-school word problems.

1. Solve: 5x − 4 = 21

2. Solve: 2(x + 3) = 16

Answer 1: 5x=25 → x=5
Answer 2: 2x+6=16 → 2x=10 → x=5
JRG has three ways to declare a value, rather like three kinds of math variable: fixed, changeable, and truly locked.

blocks.code:
package main

const TAX: float = 0.11   // never changes anywhere in the program

pub fn main() {
    let x = 5          // fixed, cannot be changed again
    let mut score = 0  // may change

    score += 10
    wok("x stays:", x)
    wok("score changed:", score)
    wok("tax is constant:", TAX)
}
blocks.output:
x stays: 5
score changed: 10
tax is constant: 0.11

blocks.title: Solving an equation = finding a variable's value
blocks.html: When a program "solves" 3x+7=22, it really runs the same algebra steps a person would: let x = (22 - 7) / 3. The computer is not "smarter" — it just runs the same steps, much faster.

blocks.question: The value of x in 4x − 3 = 17 is...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! 4x=20 → x=5.
blocks.feedbackNo: Try again: 4x = 17+3, then divide by 4.

blocks.question: If x+y=10 and x−y=4, what is x?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right! x=y+4, substitute: 2y+4=10 → y=3, x=7.
blocks.feedbackNo: Try substituting one equation into the other.

blocks.question: In JRG, a value that must NEVER change is best declared with...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! const is for values that are truly fixed, like a tax rate.
blocks.feedbackNo: Not quite — mut marks a value that MAY change.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 9
blocks.html: Now you can find x. The next chapter covers functions — "machines" that turn an input into an output consistently, written as f(x).

content.title: Math Functions
content.subtitle: A function is a consistent "machine": put something in, get a predictable result. The f(x) notation is just a formal way of writing that machine.

blocks.html: f(x) = 2x + 3 is read: "the function f, with input x, gives 2 times x plus 3." f(x) is NOT f times x — f is the name of the machine, x is what goes into it.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Reading "f(x)" as the product "f times x". But f is the function's name (like a variable name for a machine), not a number being multiplied. Compare it with sin(x) — nobody reads that as "sin times x".
The domain = every input that may go into the machine. The range = every possible result that can come out.
For example: for f(x) = 1/x, the domain is every real number except 0 — because dividing by zero is undefined (remember Chapter 3!).

1. If g(x) = x² − 1, what is g(3)?

2. If h(x) = 5, what is h(100)? (a constant function)

Answer 1: 3²−1 = 9−1 = 8
Answer 2: 5 — a constant function always returns the same value, whatever the input.

blocks.text: A function in code = a function in math

blocks.html: This is the most direct meeting point in all of the material: fn f(x: float) -> float in JRG literally is f(x) in math. Exactly the same idea — the input goes in, the rule runs, the output comes out.

blocks.title: Why this matters so much
blocks.html: Every time you call a function in a program — priceAfterDiscount() in Chapter 7, isEven() in Chapter 3 — you are already using the idea of f(x) without noticing. Functional programming is basically math run by a computer.

blocks.question: If f(x) = 3x − 2, what is f(5)?
blocks.feedbackNo: Try again: substitute x=5 into 3x−2.

blocks.question: f(x) is read as...

options.text: the function f with input x

blocks.feedbackOk: Right! f is the name of the machine/function, not a number.
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember the explanation above — f is not a number being multiplied.

blocks.question: For f(x) = 1/x, which value of x is NOT in the domain?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! x=0 would make 1/x a division by zero.
blocks.feedbackNo: Think: which value of x makes the division undefined?

blocks.title: On to Chapter 10
blocks.html: We move to applied topics: prime numbers, the GCD, and the LCM — ideas that come back in fractions (already used in Chapter 6!) and in modern cryptography.

content.title: Primes, GCD & LCM
content.subtitle: Prime numbers are the "atoms" of all integers — every other number can be broken down into a combination of primes. The GCD and the LCM come from there.

blocks.html: A prime number can only be divided evenly by 1 and itself. 1 is not prime (by mathematical agreement), and 2 is the only even prime.

blocks.title: A quick way to check for a prime
blocks.html: You only need to try dividing by the primes from 2 up to the square root of the number. If none divides evenly, it is prime. To check 97: just try 2, 3, 5, 7 (because √97≈9.8) — no need to go up to 96!

lines.html: GCD = take the smallest power of each shared factor: 2²×3¹ = 12
LCM = take the largest power of each factor that appears: 2³×3² = 72

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Mixing up the GCD and the LCM. Remember: the GCD is always ≤ both numbers (it looks for a shared factor, so it is smaller), while the LCM is always ≥ both numbers (it looks for a shared multiple, so it is bigger or equal).

1. Is 91 a prime number? (hint: try dividing by 7)

2. Find the GCD and the LCM of 18 and 30.

Answer 1: No — 91 = 7 × 13.
Answer 2: 18=2×3², 30=2×3×5 → GCD=2×3=6, LCM=2×3²×5=90.
Breaking numbers into prime factors is slow for big numbers. There is a much faster way, over 2000 years old: Euclid's algorithm — GCD(a,b) = GCD(b, a mod b), repeated until the remainder is zero.

blocks.title: Primes in the real world
blocks.html: RSA encryption, which secures online payments, relies on the fact that multiplying two large primes is easy, but taking the result apart again (factorisation) is very hard for a computer — even for numbers hundreds of digits long.

blocks.question: Which one is a prime number?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! 13 is only divisible by 1 and 13. (9=3×3, and 1 is not prime).
blocks.feedbackNo: Check: does the number have a factor other than 1 and itself?

blocks.question: The GCD of 12 and 18 is...
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember, the GCD must divide BOTH numbers evenly — check again.

blocks.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: The LCM is always ≥ both original numbers
The GCD is always ≥ both original numbers
The GCD and the LCM always have the same value

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! The LCM is a multiple, so it is always equal or bigger.
blocks.feedbackNo: Not quite — remember the opposite directions of the GCD (a factor, small) and the LCM (a multiple, big).

blocks.title: On to Chapter 11
blocks.html: Now we turn to basic statistics — how to sum up a set of data in a few key numbers that are easy to understand.

content.title: Basic Statistics
content.subtitle: Statistics is the art of summing up a mountain of data in a handful of numbers that still mean something. Four key numbers: the mean, the median, the mode, and the range.

blocks.text: Example data: test scores of 7 students

lines.html: Mean = the sum of all the data ÷ how many there are
With an even count, the median = the average of the two middle values

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Looking for the median WITHOUT sorting the data first. The median is "the middle value after sorting" — take the middle of the original (unsorted) order and the result is almost certainly wrong.

blocks.text: Mean vs median: which to trust?

blocks.html: The mean is very sensitive to extreme values (outliers); the median is not. Imagine the salaries of 5 employees: [4k, 4.5k, 5k, 5k, 50k] (the boss is included).

lines.html: Mean = (4+4.5+5+5+50)/5 = 13.7k ← misleading, nobody actually earns this
Median = 5k ← much closer to an employee's "typical salary"

blocks.title: A rule of thumb
blocks.html: If the data has extreme outliers (salaries, house prices, wealth), the median usually describes "the typical" more honestly. The mean suits fairly even data such as test scores or heights.

blocks.text: Bonus: how "spread out" is the data?

blocks.html: Two classes can have the same mean but very different spreads. The standard deviation measures this — on average, "how far" each value is from the mean.

lines.html: Both means are 80, but Class B is much more "spread out"
Class A's standard deviation is small, Class B's is large — even though the means are identical

blocks.html:
1. Data: [4, 8, 6, 8, 2]. Find the mean, median, mode, and range.

Mean: (4+8+6+8+2)/5 = 28/5 = 5.6
Median: sorted [2,4,6,8,8] → middle = 6
Mode: 8 (appears twice)
Range: 8−2 = 6

blocks.text: Computing the mean of an array

blocks.output:
Mean: 79.28571428571429
Highest score: 100.0
Lowest score: 60.0
Median: 85.0

blocks.title: This is exactly Chapter 20!
blocks.html: The mean() function above is the heart of the report-card calculator project you will build yourself later. This module is not just theory — you will use it directly.

blocks.question: Data: [3, 7, 3, 9]. What is the mode?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! 3 appears twice, more often than anything else.
blocks.feedbackNo: The mode is the value that appears MOST OFTEN, not the average.

blocks.question: When is the median more trustworthy than the mean?

options.text: When all the data is identical
The median is always better than the mean

blocks.feedbackOk: Right! The median is not pulled around by extreme values the way the mean is.
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember the employees-vs-boss salary example above.

blocks.question: Before finding the median, the data must be...

options.text: Multiplied by how many there are

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! Without sorting, "the middle value" means nothing.
blocks.feedbackNo: Read the "A common mistake" box above again.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 12
blocks.html: From number data we turn to shape and space — plane geometry: perimeter, area, and the properties of flat shapes.

content.title: Plane Geometry
content.subtitle: The perimeter measures the "distance around" a shape. The area measures "how much space" it covers. Two things that often get swapped, even though they mean very different things.

blocks.text: Perimeter & area formulas for flat shapes

blocks.title: Common mistake #1
blocks.html: Using the diameter when the formula needs the radius (r = d÷2). A circle with a diameter of 10 has r=5, not r=10 — this mistake makes the area 4× bigger than it should be.

blocks.title: Common mistake #2
blocks.html: Area units MUST be squared (cm², m²), while a perimeter keeps ordinary units (cm, m). Writing "area = 20 cm" (with no square) is a very common mistake — and it really shows a confused idea, not just a typo.

lines.html: A 12m × 8m rectangular garden, to be fenced & covered with grass

blocks.html:
1. A triangle has a base of 10cm and a height of 6cm. What is its area?

2. A circle has a diameter of 14cm (use π≈22/7). What is its area?

Answer 1: ½×10×6 = 30 cm²
Answer 2: r=7, A=22/7×7×7 = 154 cm²

blocks.title: In the real world
blocks.html: Every 2D game uses plane geometry for collision detection — checking whether two boxes or circles touch uses exactly the formulas you learn in this chapter.

blocks.question: The area of a square with 9cm sides is...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! 9² = 81 cm².
blocks.feedbackNo: The area of a square = side × side, not side × 4 (that is the perimeter).

blocks.question: A circle has a diameter of 20cm; its radius is...
blocks.feedbackOk: Right! Radius = diameter ÷ 2.
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember, the radius is always half the diameter.

blocks.question: The right unit for AREA is...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! Area is always in square units (2D).
blocks.feedbackNo: cm³ is for volume (3D), cm for length/perimeter (1D).

blocks.title: On to Chapter 13
blocks.html: Next: exponents (powers) and roots — including how bank interest grows exponentially, not linearly.

content.title: Exponents & Roots
content.subtitle: An exponent is a short way of writing repeated multiplication. A root is its opposite. Together they explain why money in the bank (and viruses, and populations) can grow much faster than intuition expects.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Thinking (a+b)² = a²+b². This is WRONG! The right one: (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b². Try it with numbers: (2+3)²=25, but 2²+3²=4+9=13. Clearly different.
This is the clearest example of how "small at the start, huge at the end" is the nature of exponents.

lines.html: $1,000 at 10% interest a year, for 20 years:
Compare that with interest WITHOUT compounding (linear): only $3,000

blocks.title: Why does it feel "suddenly fast"?
blocks.html: An exponential graph is flat at the start, then shoots up. The human brain tends to think linearly, so exponential growth (bank interest, the spread of a virus, going viral on social media) often feels surprising — even though that is simply its nature.

1. Simplify: 3⁴ × 3²

2. What is √144?

Answer 1: 3⁶ = 729
Answer 2: 12 (because 12²=144)

blocks.title: Why is it separate from the * operator?
blocks.html: A power with a decimal or variable exponent (not a small whole number) needs a special mathematical algorithm, not just repeated multiplication — that is why there is a separate math::pow() function.

blocks.question: 2⁵ equals...
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember, a power is repeated multiplication, not multiplying by the exponent.

blocks.question: (3+4)² equals...
blocks.feedbackOk: Right! (3+4)²=7²=49, NOT 3²+4².
blocks.feedbackNo: Work out the brackets first (3+4=7), then square it.

blocks.question: What is 5⁰?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! Any number (except 0) to the power 0 is always 1.
blocks.feedbackNo: This rule is a must to remember: a⁰=1.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 14
blocks.html: If an exponent answers "what is the result of this power", a logarithm answers the opposite: "what power do I need to get this result?"

content.title: Logarithms
content.subtitle: If an exponent asks "what is 2 to the power 5?", a logarithm asks the opposite: "what power must 2 be raised to, to get 32?" The answer: 5. That is log₂(32) = 5.

blocks.text: A logarithm = the reverse question of a power

blocks.title: The two logs most often written without a base
blocks.html: log(x) with no base usually means base 10 (the common log). ln(x) means base e≈2.718 (the natural log, used in calculus & science). In computer science, log₂(x) shows up most often.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: log(a+b) ≠ log(a)+log(b) — the addition rule ONLY applies to multiplication inside the log, not to addition inside the log. There is no simple formula for the log of a sum.

blocks.text: Why does log₂ matter in computer science?

blocks.html: Log₂ answers "how many times can we halve before nothing is left" — and that is exactly what happens in binary search, a method far faster than checking items one by one.

lines.html: One by one: up to 1,000,000 steps (the worst case)

blocks.html:
1. What is log₁₀(100)?

2. Simplify: log(20) − log(4)

Answer 1: 2 (because 10²=100)
Answer 2: log(20/4) = log(5)

blocks.title: Logarithmic scales around us
blocks.html: Decibels (loudness), the Richter scale (earthquake strength), and pH (acidity) are all logarithmic. A magnitude-6 earthquake is not "2× stronger" than a magnitude 3 — it is about 1000× stronger, because the scale is logarithmic.

blocks.question: log₂(16) = ?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! 2⁴=16, so log₂(16)=4.
blocks.feedbackNo: Ask: what power of 2 gives 16?

blocks.question: log(6) + log(2) equals...
blocks.feedbackOk: Right! Adding logs → multiplying inside: log(6×2)=log(12).
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember the rule: log(a)+log(b) = log(a×b).

blocks.question: Why is log₂ used so often in computer science?

options.text: Because many algorithms split data into two halves again and again
Because computers only understand the number 2

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! Like binary search, which keeps halving the data.
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember the binary-search example above.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 15
blocks.html: Next: probability — how "likely" an event is, and how to compute it exactly (not just a guess).

content.title: Probability
content.subtitle: Probability turns the word "maybe" into an exact number — between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain). In between, every uncertainty in life gets a number.

lines.html: P(A) = the number of outcomes wanted ÷ the total number of possible outcomes

blocks.html: A probability is always between 0 (not possible at all) and 1 (certain to happen). 50% = 0.5 means "equally likely to happen and not to happen."

blocks.text: AND vs OR — two formulas that get swapped

blocks.title: A common mistake: the gambler's fallacy
blocks.html: After a coin lands "Heads" 5 times in a row, many people are sure "Tails" is now more likely on the next throw. This is WRONG — every new throw is still 50-50, whatever happened before. A coin has no "memory".

1. A box holds 4 red balls and 6 blue balls. What is P(drawing a red ball)?

2. What is P(two dice BOTH show 6)?

Answer 1: 4/10 = 2/5 = 40%
Answer 2: 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36 ("both" = AND = multiply)

blocks.title: In the real world
blocks.html: Insurance companies, casinos, recommendation algorithms, and weather models all run on probability. Every time a weather app says "70% chance of rain", that is a probability computed in ways like this chapter.

blocks.question: P(rolling an even number on a die) is...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! The even numbers on a die: 2, 4, 6 = 3 of the 6 sides.
blocks.feedbackNo: Count how many even numbers there are from 1 to 6.

blocks.question: A coin is thrown 4× and lands Heads every time. The chance the 5th throw is Heads is...

options.text: More than 50%, because it is on a "lucky streak"

blocks.feedbackOk: Right! Every throw is independent — a coin does not remember earlier results.
blocks.feedbackNo: This is the gambler's fallacy — read the box above again.

blocks.question: The word "AND" in a probability problem usually means...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! AND (independent events) → multiply. OR → add.
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember the "AND vs OR" table above.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 16
blocks.html: The last four chapters before the final project widen your view: ratios & proportions, 3D solids, sequences & series, and basic trigonometry.

content.title: Ratios & Proportions
content.subtitle: A ratio compares two things relatively, not absolutely. "2 cups of flour : 1 cup of sugar" holds whether you bake 1 tray or 100 trays of cake — that is the power of a ratio.

blocks.html: The ratio 8:12 is written the same way as a fraction, and simplified the same way — divide by the GCD.
When one value goes up, the other goes up by the same factor. A recipe for 4 people has to be scaled for 10 — every ingredient grows by the same ratio.

lines.html: A recipe for 4 people needs 200g of flour. For 10 people?

blocks.html: Sometimes the link is inverse: the more workers, the less time is needed (assuming everyone works equally).

lines.html: 6 workers finish in 8 days. How many days for 4 workers?
4 workers: 48 ÷ 4 = 12 days (longer, because there are fewer people)

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Using the direct-proportion formula (multiplying straight across) on a case that is really inverse. The sign of an inverse problem: the bigger one gets, the smaller the other (workers vs time, speed vs travel time). Always ask: if one goes up, should the other go up or down?

lines.html: A map scale of 1 : 500,000. A distance on the map of 3cm; the real distance?

blocks.html:
1. Simplify the ratio 24:36.

2. A car travelling at 60km/h covers a distance in 3 hours. If its speed becomes 90km/h, how many hours does the trip take? (same distance)

Answer 1: GCD(24,36)=12 → 2:3
Answer 2: Inverse. Distance=60×3=180km. New time=180÷90=2 hours.

blocks.output:
Flour for 10 people: 500 g
Days for 4 workers: 12 days

blocks.title: Where else is it used?
blocks.html: Screen aspect ratios (16:9, 4:3), image/CSS scaling (object-fit), colour mixing (RGB), and API rate-limit budgets are all about exactly the ratios and proportions you just learned.

blocks.question: The ratio 15:25 simplifies to...
blocks.feedbackNo: Find the GCD of 15 and 25 first, then divide both.

blocks.question: 8 workers finish a project in 6 days. How many days for 12 workers?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right! Total work=8×6=48. 48÷12=4 days (inverse proportion).
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember, more workers = FEWER days.

blocks.question: The main sign of an INVERSE proportion is...

options.text: One value goes up, the other goes down

blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! Like speed vs travel time, or workers vs days.
blocks.feedbackNo: Think about the workers vs working days example above.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 17
blocks.html: The plane geometry of Chapter 12 only covered "flat" 2D shapes. Now we go up one dimension: solids — volume and surface area.

content.title: Solids
content.subtitle: Plane geometry (Chapter 12) measures flat surfaces. Solids add one more dimension: depth. Now we compute what is inside (the volume), not just the area.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Volume units MUST be cubed (cm³, m³) — not cm² (that is area) or cm (that is length). Forgetting to raise the unit's power is a sign the idea of "dimensions" is not really understood yet, not just a slip of the pen.

lines.html: A 2m × 1.5m × 1m cuboid tank, filled to the top with water
1 m³ = 1000 litres, so this tank holds 3000 litres of water

blocks.text: A cube vs a sphere of equal volume — which has the smaller surface?

blocks.html: An interesting fact: of all shapes with the same volume, the sphere has the smallest surface area. That is why water droplets, soap bubbles, and planets tend to be round — nature "saves" surface automatically.

1. A cube has 5cm sides. What is its volume?

2. A cylinder has a radius of 3cm and a height of 10cm (π≈3.14). What is its volume?

Answer 1: 5³ = 125 cm³
Answer 2: 3.14×3²×10 = 3.14×9×10 = 282.6 cm³
