blocks.title: In the real world
blocks.html: 3D graphics in games and films build every object from these basic shapes (or more complicated versions of them). Computing volume also matters for packaging, shipping (volumetric weight), and the physics engines in games.

blocks.question: The volume of a cube with 4cm sides is...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! 4³ = 4×4×4 = 64 cm³.
blocks.feedbackNo: A cube's volume = side³ (not side² or side×3).

blocks.question: Which unit is right for VOLUME?
blocks.feedbackOk: Right! Volume is always in cubed units (3D).
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember: cm=length (1D), cm²=area (2D), cm³=volume (3D).

blocks.question: A cuboid measures 3×4×5 cm. What is its volume?
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! 3×4×5 = 60 cm³.
blocks.feedbackNo: A cuboid's volume = length × width × height; multiply all of them.

blocks.title: On to Chapter 18
blocks.html: Now on to sequences & series — number patterns in order, and how to add them up without counting one by one.

content.title: Sequences & Series
content.subtitle: A sequence is a pattern of numbers in order. Once you find the pattern, you can guess the 100th term without writing the 99 before it — and add them up without adding one by one.

blocks.html: Each term comes from the one before by adding the same number (called the common difference, d).
Each term comes from the one before by multiplying by the same number (called the common ratio, r).

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Treating every sequence as arithmetic. Check first: is the DIFFERENCE between terms fixed (arithmetic), or the QUOTIENT between terms fixed (geometric)? 2,4,8,16 is not arithmetic (the differences are 2,4,8 — not fixed), but it is geometric (a fixed ratio of 2).

blocks.text: Series — the sum of all the terms

lines.html: The sum of the first 10 terms of 2,5,8,...: S₁₀ = 10/2 × (2+29) = 5×31 = 155

blocks.title: The legendary story of Gauss
blocks.html: The young mathematician Gauss was asked to add up 1 to 100. He answered 5050 at once — not by counting one by one, but by pairing (1+100), (2+99), (3+98)... which each add up to 101, 50 pairs in all: 50×101=5050. That is the heart of the arithmetic-series formula.

1. The sequence 7, 12, 17, 22, ... What is the 15th term?

2. The geometric sequence 2, 6, 18, 54, ... What is the 6th term?

Answer 1: a=7, d=5. U₁₅=7+(14×5)=7+70=77
Answer 2: a=2, r=3. U₆=2×3⁵=2×243=486

blocks.question: The sequence 4, 9, 14, 19, ... What is the 7th term?

blocks.feedbackOk: Right! A fixed ratio of ×2 at every term — that is the sign of a geometric sequence.

blocks.html: The last theory chapter: basic trigonometry — linking the angles and sides of a right triangle through sin, cos, and tan.

content.title: Basic Trigonometry
content.subtitle: Trigonometry answers the question: if we know one angle and one side of a right triangle, can we work out all the other sides & angles? The answer is yes — through sin, cos, and tan.

blocks.text: The three sides of a right triangle

blocks.html: Relative to the angle we are looking at (θ):

items.name: Hypotenuse
items.formula: Always opposite the right angle, always the longest

items.name: Opposite
items.formula: The side across from the angle θ

items.name: Adjacent
items.formula: The side touching the angle θ (not the hypotenuse)

blocks.title: SOH-CAH-TOA
blocks.html: Sin=Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cos=Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tan=Opposite/Adjacent. Read the first letter of each word: S-O-H, C-A-H, T-O-A.

blocks.text: An example: measuring a height without climbing

lines.html: The angle of elevation to the top of a pole = 60°, standing 20m away

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.html: Swapping the "opposite" and "adjacent" sides — both are relative to the angle being used, not fixed positions in the picture. If the known angle moves to another angle of the same triangle, which side is "opposite" and which "adjacent" changes too!

1. A right triangle has opposite=3 and adjacent=4. How long is the hypotenuse? (hint: Pythagoras)

2. A 10m ladder leans at 45° to the ground. How high is the top of the ladder above the ground?

Answer 1: √(3²+4²)=√25=5
Answer 2: sin(45°)=height/10 → height=10×0.707≈7.07m

blocks.text: Trigonometric functions — watch out for radians!

blocks.html: The functions math::sin/cos/tan in JRG (as in most programming languages) take angles in radians, not degrees. The conversion: radians = degrees × (π/180).

blocks.title: A classic beginner bug
blocks.html: Calling math::sin(60.0) directly without converting to radians — the result is COMPLETELY WRONG, because 60 is taken as 60 radians (more than 9 full turns!), not 60°. This is one of the most common trigonometry bugs in every programming language.

blocks.question: sin θ is defined as...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! SOH: Sin = Opposite/Hypotenuse.
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember SOH-CAH-TOA — sin always has the hypotenuse below the line.

blocks.question: tan θ is defined as...
blocks.feedbackOk: Right! TOA: Tan = Opposite/Adjacent.
blocks.feedbackNo: Tan does not involve the hypotenuse at all — check TOA again.

blocks.question: Before calling math::sin() in JRG, an angle in degrees must be...
blocks.feedbackOk: Exactly! radians = degrees × (π/180).
blocks.feedbackNo: Remember the classic bug above — trig functions in code use radians, not degrees.

content.title: Project: Report-Card Calculator
content.subtitle: Where the whole journey meets. This project combines statistics (Chapter 11), functions (Chapter 9), and variables (Chapter 8) into one genuinely useful tool: an automatic report-card calculator.

blocks.html: Put in a few test scores. The tool computes the average (mean), the median, the highest & lowest scores, then decides a letter grade from the average — every idea you mastered one by one in the earlier chapters, now working together.
This program uses ideas from Chapters 8, 9, and 11 at once: functions, loops, the mean, and the median.

blocks.title: Try it with your own scores
blocks.html: Press Edit, replace the contents of scores with your own report-card scores, then press Run. When you are done, mark this project as finished with the button below.

blocks.title: Congratulations on finishing all the material!
blocks.html: From getting to know numbers in Chapter 1 to computing grades automatically here, you have been through 20 full chapters — arithmetic, algebra, statistics, 2D & 3D geometry, exponents, logarithms, probability, sequences, and trigonometry. More importantly: you have seen every idea twice — as math and as code that really runs. Keep that habit — math and programming logic will keep strengthening each other wherever you go on to learn.

blocks.title: Why Kotlin matters
blocks.html: Kotlin is the main language for Android apps, and its ecosystem is large. Because Kotlin runs on the JVM, JRG calls it the same way as Java — what differs is only the NAMES its compiler uses: functions in a file Calc.kt land in a class CalcKt, and an object becomes a field named INSTANCE.

blocks.title: Building apps with JRG
blocks.html: Besides FFI, JRG has dok:: — more than a hundred functions for building applications: an HTTP router, WebSocket, SQLite, templates that escape HTML themselves, signed cookies, and password hashing. A complete example is in the repo: examples/web_app_demo.jrg.
